chapter: Branches of Philosophy: Epistemology and Metaphysics
trick: Three questions, three branches. What exists? — metaphysics. How do we know? — epistemology. What ought we to do? — ethics. Any term in this chapter can be placed by asking which of those three questions it answers.

video.query: branches of philosophy epistemology metaphysics ethics class 11

data.prompt: Which branch of philosophy does each question belong to?

items.label: Is reality ultimately one or many?
Can the senses give certain knowledge?
Is an action right because of its consequences?
Does this conclusion follow from these premises?
What is the nature of the soul?
What is the difference between belief and knowledge?
What makes a life a good life?
What is a valid syllogism?

trick: Charvaka accepts perception alone as a source of knowledge, and everything else follows from that one refusal — no inference, so no unseen soul, no afterlife, no God, and four elements rather than five, because ether is never perceived. It is the only openly materialist school, and the only nastika school that rejects the Vedas outright and offers nothing spiritual in return.

video.query: charvaka lokayata materialism indian philosophy class 11

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about Charvaka.

items.statement: Charvaka accepts perception (pratyaksha) as the only valid source of knowledge.
items.why: It rejects inference and testimony, because both take you beyond what is actually seen.

items.statement: Charvaka accepts five elements, including ether.
items.why: It accepts only four — earth, water, fire and air. Ether is never perceived, so by its own rule it cannot be admitted.

items.statement: Charvaka is an astika school because it is Indian.
items.why: Astika and nastika turn on whether the Vedas are accepted as authority, not on being Indian. Charvaka, Buddhism and Jainism are all nastika.

items.statement: Charvaka holds that consciousness arises from matter.
items.why: As the power to intoxicate arises when ingredients are fermented, consciousness is said to arise when the elements combine in a body — and ends with it.

items.statement: Charvaka is also known as Lokayata.
items.why: Lokayata means 'of this world', which is exactly the school's position: this world is all there is.

trick: Both are nastika, both teach ahimsa, and questions exploit the overlap — so hold on to what is unique. Buddhism: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, momentariness, no permanent soul. Jainism: three jewels, seven tattvas, syadvada, and a soul (jiva) that very much exists. When a question offers a doctrine both could claim, look for the word that decides it.

video.query: buddhism four noble truths jainism syadvada anekantavada class 11 philosophy

data.prompt: Which school does each doctrine belong to? Some belong to both.

items.label: The Four Noble Truths
The three jewels: right faith, knowledge, conduct
Ahimsa as a central principle
Anatta — there is no permanent self
Syadvada — every judgement is conditional
Rejection of the authority of the Vedas
The doctrine of momentariness (kshanikavada)
Anekantavada — reality has many aspects
The theory of dependent origination
Liberation from the cycle of rebirth as the goal

trick: The four parts of Vedic literature run in order of life as much as of text: Samhita the hymns, Brahmana the ritual, Aranyaka the forest, Upanishad the philosophy. Vedanta means literally 'the end of the Vedas' — it is the Upanishads, and that is why Vedanta is the philosophical part and not a separate book.

video.query: vedas samhita brahmana aranyaka upanishad vedanta class 11 philosophy

data.prompt: Match each term with what it means.

pairs.right: The collection of hymns — the oldest layer
Prose explaining the performance of sacrifice and ritual
The 'forest texts', bridging ritual and philosophy
The philosophical conclusion of the Vedas — Vedanta
The earliest Veda, hymns of praise
The Veda of melodies and chants
The ultimate reality underlying everything
The self, held by Vedanta to be one with Brahman

trick: Plato is the rationalist: real knowledge is of eternal Forms, and the senses only show shadows. Locke is the empiricist: the mind begins as a blank slate, tabula rasa, and every idea arrives through experience. They answer the same question — where does knowledge come from — in exactly opposite ways.

video.query: plato theory of forms locke tabula rasa empiricism rationalism class 11

data.prompt: Sort each idea by the thinker it belongs to.

items.label: The Theory of Forms or Ideas
The mind at birth is a tabula rasa
The Allegory of the Cave
All ideas come from sensation and reflection
Knowledge is recollection of what the soul already knew
The distinction between primary and secondary qualities
The senses give only opinion, not knowledge
There are no innate ideas

chapter: Philosophy of Education and Educational Thinkers
trick: Each philosophy hands education a different aim, and the aim gives away the school. Idealism aims at spiritual self-realisation, naturalism at growth by nature's own plan, pragmatism at solving real problems by doing. Match the aim to the -ism and the method follows on its own.

video.query: idealism naturalism pragmatism philosophy of education class 11

data.prompt: Match each philosophy of education with what it holds.

pairs.right: Education aims at self-realisation and the development of spiritual values
Follow nature; the child grows by its own law and the teacher does not interfere
Truth is what works; education is learning by doing and by solving problems
The world exists independently of the mind, so teach it as it is, through the senses
Naturalism — Emile, the child left to nature's own schooling
Pragmatism — education is life itself, not preparation for life
Idealism — turning the soul towards the Good

trick: Three experiments, three theories, and the animal tells you which is which. A dog and a bell is Pavlov's classical conditioning. A cat in a puzzle box is Thorndike's trial and error. A rat pressing a lever for food is Skinner's operant conditioning. Kohler's apes reaching a banana are the insight theory that rejects trial and error altogether.

video.query: pavlov thorndike skinner kohler theories of learning class 11 psychology

data.prompt: Match each theorist with the experiment and the idea it produced.

pairs.right: A dog salivating at a bell — classical conditioning
A cat escaping a puzzle box — learning by trial and error
A rat pressing a lever for food — operant conditioning and reinforcement
An ape joining sticks to reach a banana — learning by insight
Thorndike: responses followed by satisfaction are repeated
Thorndike: a connection strengthens with practice and weakens without it
The food, which produces the response without any learning
Anything that makes a response more likely to occur again
